Attempt 1 failed immediately on a cargo-mutants argument-passing mistake (--test-threads not properly separated for the underlying cargo test invocation -- operator error, not a code defect). PARTIAL: encryption.rs 9/10 mutants caught (90%, healthy) when correctly scoped to its actual integration-test coverage (tests/secrets_management, decrypt_with_rotation direct-call tests) -- the sole survivor is a benign boundary-equivalent mutant (ciphertext.len() < 12 vs <= 12; both behave identically for any real AES-GCM input since the 16-byte tag makes exactly-12-bytes impossible). config.rs's 71-mutant run (many MISSED, concentrated in resolve_admin_key/resolve_encryption_key_hex/resolve_admin_key_previous/resolve_encryption_key_previous_hex) used --lib scope, which excludes the acceptance suite where these functions' real precedence/ambiguity behavior is actually exercised end-to-end via ServerProcess subprocess tests -- same class of scoping mistake initially made on encryption.rs. Attempted manual validation (mutate one guard, rebuild --bin embyr-server, rerun the AWS walking-skeleton acceptance scenario) to determine if the acceptance suite actually catches these mutants, but hit a reproducible environmental TLS failure (aws-smithy-http-client native-roots cert loading, 'no valid root certificates parsed') on 3 of 4 attempts, unrelated to the mutation itself -- every attempt with the mutation genuinely applied crashed on this unrelated setup step before reaching the real assertion. No clean signal obtained either way for config.rs. User decision: FINALIZE now, log this as inconclusive follow-up rather than block on it -- 28/29 real acceptance scenarios plus an approved adversarial security review are stronger practical evidence of correctness than a mutation run that was both mis-scoped and then blocked by an unrelated environment issue. Follow-up: re-run config.rs mutation testing with correct scope (--test secrets_management, not --lib) on a machine without the TLS cert-loading instability; separately worth investigating whether that TLS flakiness could recur for real users hitting AWS Secrets Manager in production.
